items.prompt: What does APR stand for on a loan or credit card statement?

options.label: Annual Percentage Rate
Applied Principal Return
Average Payment Record
Annual Premium Refund

rubric: APR is the Annual Percentage Rate, the yearly cost of borrowing.
Distractors invent plausible finance-sounding terms.

items.prompt: In the common 50/30/20 budgeting guideline, how is after-tax income split?

options.label: 40% needs, 40% wants, 20% taxes and insurance only
50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and debt repayment
50% wants, 30% needs, 20% savings and debt repayment
50% savings, 30% needs, 20% wants and entertainment

rubric: The rule is 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and debt repayment.
Distractors swap the categories or the percentages.

items.prompt: What is the term for the regular payment you make to keep an insurance policy active?

options.label: Principal
Deductible
Premium
Beneficiary

rubric: A premium is the recurring payment for coverage.
Deductible is the amount paid before coverage begins, a common mix-up.

items.prompt: A commonly recommended size for a starter-to-full emergency fund is how much?

options.label: Two months of your total credit card limit
A full year of all spending including luxuries
3 to 6 months of essential living expenses
One week of take-home pay kept in cash

rubric: The standard guideline is 3 to 6 months of essential expenses.
Distractors use amounts that are too small, too large, or based on credit rather than cash.

items.prompt: What is a credit score?

options.label: The total amount of money you currently owe across all of your lenders
The interest rate a bank pays you on your savings balance
A number that summarizes how reliably you have repaid borrowed money
Your yearly income as reported to the tax authority each spring

rubric: A credit score summarizes repayment history and credit behavior.
Distractors confuse it with debt total, income, or savings rate.

items.prompt: Which of these are typically fixed expenses in a monthly budget? Select all that apply.

options.label: Insurance premium
Monthly rent
Dining out
Car loan payment
Grocery bill

rubric: Rent, loan payments and premiums are the same amount each month.
Dining out and groceries vary month to month, so they are variable.

items.prompt: Maya starts her first job with a stated salary of 3,000 per month. Her first paycheck deposit is only 2,450 after income tax and other deductions were taken out. What is the term for the 2,450 amount she actually receives?

options.label: Total premium
Gross pay
Net pay
Taxable income

rubric: Net pay, or take-home pay, is what remains after deductions.
Gross pay is the amount before deductions, the most common confusion.

items.prompt: Why does paying more than the minimum on a credit card save money?

options.label: Interest is charged on the unpaid balance, so extra payments cut total interest
Extra payments raise your credit limit, which lowers the rate you are charged
Lenders refund the first year of interest once payments exceed the minimum
Paying extra turns the card debt into a savings balance that earns interest

rubric: Interest accrues on the remaining balance, so a faster payoff means less interest.
Distractors describe benefits that credit cards do not provide.

items.prompt: What does choosing an insurance plan with a higher deductible usually mean?

options.label: A lower premium, and the insurer pays every claim from the first dollar
A lower premium, but more out-of-pocket cost before coverage pays
A higher premium, and the insurer pays every claim from the first dollar
A higher premium, but more out-of-pocket cost before coverage pays

rubric: A higher deductible shifts early costs to you in exchange for a lower premium.
Distractors reverse the premium relationship or ignore what a deductible is.

items.prompt: Why is it generally advised to start saving for retirement early rather than late?

options.label: Earnings are reinvested and grow on themselves, so more time multiplies the savings
Retirement accounts only accept deposits made before the age of thirty
Early savers are exempt from paying income tax on their final pension
Interest rates on retirement accounts fall every year you wait to open one

rubric: Compound growth rewards time in the market.
Distractors state false rules about eligibility, taxes or rates.

items.prompt: A credit card charges 24% APR. If you carry a 1,000 balance for a year without paying it down, roughly how much interest do you owe?

options.label: About 120
About 240
About 24
About 2,400

rubric: 24% of 1,000 is about 240 per year, slightly more with monthly compounding.
Other options come from misplacing the decimal or halving the rate.

items.prompt: Your income stays the same and you add a new 100 monthly subscription without cutting any other spending. What is the most likely result?

options.label: Your income rises by 100 to cover the new cost
Your emergency fund grows by 100 each month
Your fixed expenses fall because the total is spread out
You have 100 less each month for savings or other goals

rubric: With fixed income, each new expense reduces what is left over.
Distractors assume income or savings adjust automatically.

items.prompt: Which habits tend to help build a stronger credit score? Select all that apply.

options.label: Applying for many new cards in a short time
Carrying a card at its maximum limit each month
Paying bills on or before the due date
Keeping card balances low relative to your limits

rubric: On-time payment and low utilization both signal reliable borrowing.
Many applications and maxed-out cards signal risk and lower the score.

items.prompt: Jon's employer matches 50% of his retirement contributions, up to 6% of his salary. Jon contributes only 2% of his salary because he wants to keep more cash each month. How best can his choice be described?

options.label: He is giving up part of the employer match, which is extra pay for saving
He is receiving the full match, since any contribution qualifies him for it
He is protecting his credit score, since employers report contributions
He is avoiding all tax on his salary, since small amounts are never taxed

rubric: The match applies up to 6%, so contributing 2% leaves matching money unclaimed.
Distractors misread how matches, taxes and credit reporting work.

items.prompt: Why is an emergency fund usually kept in an easily accessible savings account rather than invested in stocks?

options.label: Savings accounts always earn higher returns than stocks, so they grow faster over time
Interest on savings is tax-free, which stocks never are, so savings keep more money
Stock prices may be low when cash is needed, so the money could be worth less
Stocks cannot be sold at all for several weeks, so the money would be locked up

rubric: Emergency money must hold its value and be available on short notice; stocks can be down when an emergency hits.
Distractors rely on false claims that savings always out-earn stocks or that stocks cannot be sold.

items.prompt: A person pays only the minimum payment on a credit card each month and adds no new purchases. What is the usual result?

options.label: The issuer reports the account as delinquent, since less than the full balance was paid
Interest stops for the month, since a payment was made on or before the due date
Interest keeps accruing on the unpaid balance, so the debt lasts longer and costs more
The balance drops fast, since the minimum covers all interest and most of the principal

rubric: Minimum payments cover mostly interest, so the balance shrinks slowly and total cost rises.
Distractors confuse minimum payments with full payment or with a missed payment.

items.prompt: Which of these is a fixed expense in a monthly budget?

options.label: Dining out
Electricity bill
Monthly rent set by a lease
Weekly grocery spending

rubric: A fixed expense stays the same each month, like rent under a lease.
Groceries, utilities and dining vary with use or choice.

items.prompt: In an insurance policy, what does the deductible mean?

options.label: The share of each bill you pay after the insurer has reached its limit
The most the insurer will pay out for a single covered loss
The amount you pay toward a covered loss before the insurer starts paying
The fixed amount you pay every month to keep the policy active

rubric: The deductible is the out-of-pocket amount paid before coverage begins.
Distractors confuse it with the premium, the coverage limit, or coinsurance.

items.prompt: A worker receives a large income tax refund after filing. What does this most likely indicate?

options.label: Your income was taxed at a lower rate than the law sets for other workers
Too little tax was withheld, so the government is returning the shortfall to you
The government rewards taxpayers who file early with a bonus payment on top of their tax
More tax was withheld than you owed, so you gave the government an interest-free loan

rubric: A refund means over-withholding during the year; the extra money earned no interest for you.
Distractors misread refunds as shortfalls, special rates, or early-filing bonuses.

items.prompt: Which of the following typically influence a credit score? Select all that apply.

options.label: Your annual salary
Your checking account balance
How much of your credit limit you use
Whether bills are paid on time

rubric: Payment history and credit utilization are core scoring factors.
Income and bank balances are not part of credit reports, a common misconception.

items.prompt: Maya keeps $2,000 in a savings account paying 1% a year. Over the same year, prices for everyday goods rise about 4%. At the end of the year, what has happened to what her savings can buy?

options.label: It has fallen, because prices rose faster than her interest accrued
It is unchanged, because inflation affects only prices and not savings accounts
It has risen, because her balance grew and a larger balance always buys more
It is unchanged, because the account balance is insured against rising prices

rubric: Real purchasing power falls when inflation exceeds the interest rate.
Distractors confuse a growing nominal balance with growing buying power.

items.prompt: Your monthly after-tax income is $3,000. Using the 50/30/20 guideline (needs/wants/savings and debt repayment), how much goes to savings and debt repayment?
rubric: Other values come from applying 10%, 30%, or 50% by mistake.

items.prompt: Essential monthly expenses are $2,200. The goal is an emergency fund covering 3 months of essentials, and $1,500 is already saved. How much more is needed?
rubric: Distractors skip the subtraction or use the wrong number of months.

items.prompt: A credit card has a $1,000 balance and a 24% APR, compounded monthly. About how much interest is charged for one month if nothing is paid?
rubric: Distractors use the annual rate for a month or misplace the decimal.

items.prompt: An employer matches 50% of your contributions to a retirement plan, up to 6% of salary. Your salary is $60,000 and you contribute 4%. How much does the employer add per year?
rubric: Your 4% is $2,400; a 50% match adds $1,200.
$1,800 assumes you contributed the full 6%; $2,400 assumes a 100% match.

items.prompt: You have an extra $200 a month for debt. Debts: Card A $400 at 9%, Card B $2,500 at 24%, Loan C $6,000 at 5%. To minimize total interest, where should the extra money go after minimums are paid?

options.label: The $6,000 loan at 5%
The $2,500 balance at 24%
Split equally among all three debts
The $400 balance at 9%

rubric: The avalanche method targets the highest interest rate first, which is Card B.
Paying the smallest balance first is the snowball method, which can cost more interest.

items.prompt: Dana wants to smooth out irregular costs by setting aside a little each month in a sinking fund. Which of these expenses suit that approach? Select all that apply.

options.label: Yearly holiday gifts
The weekly grocery shop
Monthly rent
A $600 annual car insurance premium

rubric: Sinking funds suit predictable but infrequent costs such as annual premiums and gifts.
Groceries and rent are regular monthly costs paid from the normal budget.

items.prompt: Priya takes home $3,200 a month. Her fixed costs are rent $1,100, utilities $200, groceries $400, transport $300 and minimum debt payments $150. She wants to save $600 a month. How much is left for wants?
rubric: Distractors forget to subtract the savings or some of the expenses.

items.prompt: Maria's take-home pay is $3,200 a month. She uses a 50/30/20 budget: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and debt repayment. How much should go to savings and debt repayment each month?
rubric: $960 is the wants share and $1,600 is the needs share, which come from mixing up the categories.

items.prompt: Monthly spending: rent $1,200, food $400, utilities $150, transport $250, insurance $200, entertainment $600. Sam wants an emergency fund of 3 months of essential expenses. He has $2,000 saved and adds $550 a month. How many months of saving (rounded up) until he reaches the goal?

options.label: 9 months
12 months
6 months
8 months

rubric: Essentials total $2,200, so the goal is $6,600; the $4,600 gap divided by $550 is 8.4, rounded up to 9.
12 months comes from counting entertainment as essential; 8 comes from rounding down.

items.prompt: A credit card charges 24% APR as 2% per month on the balance. The balance is $2,000 at the start of the month, there are no new purchases, and you pay $100 at month end. What is the balance after the payment?
rubric: $1,900 ignores interest; $2,040 ignores the payment's effect on the balance.

items.prompt: Debts: card $3,000 at 24% APR, store card $1,200 at 15%, personal loan $800 at 6%. All minimums are paid and she has $200 extra each month. To minimise total interest paid, where should the extra $200 go?

options.label: The 24% card, because each dollar owed there costs the most in interest
The 15% store card, because it sits in the middle and balances cost and speed
The 6% loan, because its small balance can be cleared fastest
Split evenly across all three, because interest is charged on every balance

rubric: The avalanche method targets the highest rate first to minimise interest.
Targeting the smallest balance is the snowball method, which is motivating but not the cheapest.

items.prompt: A country taxes the first $10,000 of taxable income at 10% and the portion above $10,000, up to $40,000, at 20%. Priya's taxable income is $30,000. How much income tax does she owe?
rubric: Tax is $1,000 on the first $10,000 plus $4,000 on the next $20,000, which is $5,000.
$6,000 applies 20% to everything; $4,000 forgets the first band.

items.prompt: A freelancer's monthly income varies between $2,000 and $4,000. Which steps correctly apply a budget method for irregular income? Select all that apply.

options.label: Cover lean-month shortfalls with credit card borrowing
Base the monthly budget on your lowest typical month's income
Set the budget using your best month so goals are met sooner
Move income above that baseline into a buffer account in strong months
Pay yourself a fixed monthly amount from the buffer account

rubric: Budgeting on a low baseline, saving surpluses and paying a steady amount smooths irregular income.
Budgeting on the best month or borrowing in lean months creates shortfalls and debt.

items.prompt: Dev earns $48,000 a year. His employer matches 100% of his retirement contributions up to 5% of salary. Dev currently contributes 3% of his salary and is reviewing his pay slip. How much employer match does he leave unclaimed each year?
rubric: The maximum match is 5% of $48,000 = $2,400; he receives 3% = $1,440, so $960 is unclaimed.
$1,440 is what he already gets; $2,400 is the full match.

items.prompt: A household's budget plans spending of $2,900 against $3,000 monthly take-home pay, yet its card balance rises about $250 every month. Which is the most likely cause?

options.label: The card's interest rate is higher than the rate assumed when the plan was written
Planned spending that nearly matches income always triggers automatic card borrowing
Bills fall due on uneven dates, which adds extra charges on top of the plan each month
Irregular costs like car repairs, gifts and annual fees were left out of the plan

rubric: Unbudgeted non-monthly expenses are the usual hidden source of a gap between plan and reality.
The other options describe effects that are not the typical cause of a steady monthly gap.

items.prompt: Loan A: 5.0% APR, no fees, 5 years. Loan B: 4.5% interest rate, a 2% origination fee deducted from the amount received, 5 years. You need the same usable amount from either. Which comparison method correctly shows which is cheaper?

options.label: Compare total cost including the fee over the full term, or an APR that includes the fee
Pick the loan with the lower monthly payment, since the fee is not part of repayment
Compare the headline rates only, because a one-time fee is small next to years of interest
Pick the loan with the fee, because a fee signals a lender with lower default risk

rubric: Fees raise the effective cost, so comparison must include them.
Headline rate or monthly payment alone ignores the fee's effect.

items.prompt: A healthy 28-year-old says: "I'll skip health insurance, which costs $300 a month, and just save $300 a month instead." What is the main flaw in this reasoning?

options.label: Premiums always cost less than expected claims, so saved money can never match insurance cover
Healthy people cannot legally self-insure, so the plan fails whatever it costs overall
Interest on the savings is taxed, so $300 a month would lose value faster than premiums
A single serious claim could exceed the savings, and insurance pools that rare, large risk

rubric: Insurance protects against low-probability, high-cost events that savings accumulate too slowly to cover.
Distractors rely on false claims about premiums, taxes or legality.

items.prompt: Sam paid off his oldest credit card and closed it. His score then fell 30 points even though he never missed a payment. He still carries balances on his other cards. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Closing the account triggers a hard inquiry on his report that lowers the score permanently afterwards
Closing it cut total available credit, raising utilisation, and removed his longest account history
Closed accounts lose their payment history at once, so his on-time record disappeared from his report
Paying off a card sends an automatic alert to lenders that lowers scores for some months afterwards

rubric: Lower total limits raise utilisation on remaining balances, and losing the oldest account shortens average history.
Paying off or closing does not create a hard inquiry, and closed accounts in good standing usually stay on the report.

items.prompt: Gross income is $5,000 a month. A lender caps total debt payments, including the new $1,600 mortgage payment, at 43% of gross income. Existing payments: car $400, student loan $300, card minimum $100, giving 48%. He can clear only one of the student loan or the card. Which change gets under the cap?

options.label: Pay off the card, which removes its $100 payment and also gives about 42%
Pay off the student loan, which removes its $300 payment and gives about 42%
Raise his credit score by 40 points, which lenders subtract from the DTI percentage
Close the card without paying it, which removes its minimum from the DTI calculation

rubric: Removing $300 leaves $2,100 of payments, which is 42% of $5,000; removing $100 leaves 46%.
Credit score changes and closing an unpaid card do not alter the debt payments counted in DTI.

items.prompt: A household reviews six months of spending against its budget. Which findings point to a structural problem with the budget rather than a one-off overspend? Select all that apply.

options.label: Fixed costs make up 70% of take-home pay, leaving little room to adjust
A one-time car repair in March pushed that month over budget
Groceries ran over the planned amount in five of the six months
A holiday gift month in December exceeded the usual spending

rubric: Repeated overruns and a very high fixed-cost share show the plan itself is unrealistic or inflexible.
A single repair or a seasonal gift month is a one-off that a sinking fund can handle.

items.prompt: Lena owes $5,000 on a card with a 24% APR, charged as 2% per month. She pays $150 each month and makes no new purchases. After her first payment the balance is about $4,950, and she worries the payment is doing almost nothing. Which best explains this?

options.label: Her payment was applied to fees before the balance, so none of it reduced what she owes
Interest is charged on the payment amount, so the $150 added a further charge to her debt
Card issuers apply the first payment to next month's interest, so the principal falls faster later
About $100 of the payment covered that month's interest, so only about $50 reduced the balance

rubric: Monthly interest is 2% of $5,000 = $100, leaving $50 to reduce principal, so the balance becomes $4,950.
The distractors invent payment-allocation rules that do not match how the balance changed.

items.prompt: A couple takes home $5,000 a month. Their budget app shows categorized spending of $4,600, yet their savings balance grows only $100 a month. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: Price inflation during the month makes the $4,600 figure outdated by the time it is totaled
Their savings account interest rate is too low to account for the missing $400 each month
A $100 monthly surplus is normal because a budget should leave only about two percent unspent
Cash withdrawals and annual bills sit outside the app's categories, so real spending is near $4,900

rubric: Untracked cash and irregular annual costs are the usual leak when categorized totals do not match the savings change.
Distractors blame interest or inflation, which are far too small to explain a $300 gap.

items.prompt: Lena pays her card in full every month. After a month when she charged $2,800 on a $3,000 limit, her credit score dipped, even though she paid on the due date. Why?

options.label: Paying in full tells scoring models she never carries debt, which lowers her score slightly
The issuer reported the statement balance before her payment, so utilization looked near 93 percent
The payment triggered a hard inquiry on her file, which cut her score for that month
Paying on the due date counts as late when it falls after the statement closing date

rubric: Utilization is usually measured on the balance reported at statement close, regardless of later payment.
Distractors confuse the due date with the closing date or invent penalties for paying in full.

items.prompt: Sam is $1,000 below the top of a tax bracket and gets a $3,000 raise, so $2,000 of it lands in the next marginal bracket. Sam fears take-home pay will fall. Which analysis is correct?

options.label: The higher rate applies to the full $3,000 raise, though net pay still rises by a smaller amount
Take-home falls whenever the raise is smaller than the width of the bracket Sam has crossed into
The higher rate applies to all of Sam's income, so take-home falls if the rate jump is large enough
The higher rate applies only to the $2,000 above the threshold, so take-home pay still rises

rubric: Marginal rates tax only the income inside each bracket, so a raise cannot reduce net pay through bracket crossing alone.
Distractors reflect the belief that the new rate applies to all income or to the entire raise.

items.prompt: A household has $4,000 on a card at 22% APR and $9,000 on a loan at 7% APR, minimums paid on both, plus $300 a month extra. A friend says payoff order is irrelevant because total payments are equal. What is the flaw?

options.label: Order matters only when the minimums differ, since compounding then changes between the two debts
Extra dollars on the larger balance cut principal faster, so total interest is lower over the repayment
Extra dollars on the 22% balance stop the costliest interest sooner, so total interest paid is lower
Order affects only credit score, because the interest on each debt is fixed when it is first taken

rubric: Interest accrues at each debt's own rate, so directing extra money to the highest rate minimizes total interest.
Distractors treat balance size or minimums as the driver instead of the rate.

items.prompt: Raising a car insurance deductible from $500 to $2,000 cuts the premium by $480 a year. Which comparison decides whether the change is sound?

options.label: Whether she can cover the extra $1,500 and expects claims less often than about every three years
Whether the $480 saved beats the rate at which prices rise on her yearly spending
Whether the insurer's claims-paying rating tends to improve when deductibles are higher
Whether the $480 saved is bigger than the $500 deductible she had before the change

rubric: The extra $1,500 exposure divided by $480 saved gives roughly a three-year break-even, plus the need to afford the deductible.
Distractors use irrelevant benchmarks such as inflation, insurer ratings or the old deductible.

items.prompt: A freelancer and a salaried employee have identical monthly expenses. Which factors justify a larger emergency fund for the freelancer? Select all that apply.

options.label: Late client payments can leave weeks with no cash arriving at all
Freelancers' fixed expenses are always higher than those of salaried workers
Self-employed workers usually have no employer sick pay or paid leave to fall back on
Income can swing month to month, so shortfalls occur without any job loss

rubric: Variable income, payment gaps and missing employer benefits all raise the cash buffer needed.
The distractor assumes expenses differ by employment type, which the prompt rules out.

items.prompt: Maria earns $60,000. Her employer matches 50% of her contributions up to 6% of pay. She contributes 3% and carries card debt at 24% APR. She plans to stop contributing and send that money to the card. What is the key flaw in her plan?

options.label: Dropping to 0% forfeits an instant 50% match return, which beats the 24% interest she would save
Retirement money is locked away, so she would lack liquidity to pay the card down later
Paying the card first lowers her credit utilization, which she would then have to rebuild
Card interest at 24% is tax-deductible, so paying the card faster saves less than it appears

rubric: An employer match is an immediate guaranteed return that exceeds the card's interest rate, so it should be captured.
Distractors invoke a false tax deduction, liquidity or credit effects that do not change the comparison.

items.prompt: Priya, 28, is in the 12% bracket and expects to be in the 24% bracket in retirement. She does not need a deduction now and wants to minimize lifetime tax on retirement savings. Which contribution type best meets her criteria?

options.label: Traditional contributions, since a deduction now is worth more than tax-free withdrawals later
Taxable brokerage investing, because it avoids all retirement account rules and tax drag
Roth contributions, paying 12% now to avoid 24% tax on withdrawals
Traditional contributions, because the tax rate on withdrawals will match her current rate

rubric: Paying tax at a lower rate now and avoiding a higher rate later minimizes lifetime tax.
Distractors ignore the expected rate difference or assume the rates will match.

items.prompt: A household has a full emergency fund and captures its employer match. Its goal is to be debt-free in 8 years with the least chance of missing that date, and its risk tolerance is low. Extra cash can prepay a 5.5% fixed mortgage or buy stock index funds. Which is best?

options.label: Invest in index funds, because stocks have beaten 5.5% over every 8-year period on record
Hold the cash in savings, because prepayment is irreversible and cash earns more than 5.5%
Invest in index funds, because the higher expected return outweighs volatility for any goal
Prepay the mortgage, since a certain 5.5% return suits a low risk tolerance and a fixed deadline

rubric: A guaranteed return that meets the deadline fits the stated criteria of low risk and a fixed target date.
Distractors assert stock outperformance as certain or ignore the risk criterion.

items.prompt: A single-earner family of four has a $300,000 mortgage, a three-month emergency fund and employer health insurance, but no life or disability coverage. Judging by size of potential loss and inability to cover it from savings, which gap is the most serious?

options.label: No umbrella liability policy, since lawsuits are more likely than death or disability
No life or disability coverage on the sole earner, since losses far exceed their savings
No home warranty plan, since repair costs recur more often than any income loss
An emergency fund of three months rather than six, since job loss is the likeliest shock

rubric: Loss of the only income would be catastrophic and cannot be absorbed by a three-month fund.
Distractors rank by frequency or minor cost rather than severity against the stated criteria.

items.prompt: Dana nets $3,000 a month in a high-cost city and pays $1,650 rent (55%). She wants to stay solvent and keep saving. Which critique of applying the 50/30/20 rule literally is strongest?

options.label: The rule works if she simply relabels rent as a want, which brings needs under 50%
The rule is sound, so she should break her lease and move somewhere cheaper right away
Needs already exceed 50%, so she should set a savings floor, trim wants and adapt the ratios
She should skip saving until needs fall below 50%, to avoid taking on any new debt

rubric: The ratios are a heuristic; with fixed costs above 50%, adjusting wants while keeping a savings floor meets her criteria.
Distractors force the template, relabel costs or abandon saving.

items.prompt: An emergency fund must be reachable within one or two business days, must not lose principal, and should earn some interest. Which place best meets all three criteria?

options.label: A long-term bond fund, because its yield exceeds savings rates
A high-yield savings account at an insured bank
A broad stock index fund, because it earns the most over time
A five-year CD, because it pays the highest rate available

rubric: An insured high-yield savings account is liquid, principal-stable and pays interest.
Distractors give up liquidity or principal stability for yield.

items.prompt: A friend proposes holding the whole emergency fund in stock index funds for higher returns. Which are sound criticisms of this plan? Select all that apply.

options.label: The fund's purpose is to cover shocks reliably, so volatility defeats it despite a higher expected return
Index funds cannot be sold quickly, so the money is locked up for several years
She may be forced to sell at a loss, turning a temporary dip into a permanent shortfall
Stock prices often fall in recessions, when job loss makes the fund most likely to be needed

rubric: Correlated downturns, forced sales and purpose mismatch are valid criticisms.
Index funds are generally sellable within days, so the lock-up claim is false.

items.prompt: Jo receives a $10,000 windfall. She owes $3,000 on a card at 21% APR and $8,000 on a car loan at 4%. Her emergency fund holds $500 against monthly needs of $3,000. Her criteria are to remove the costliest debt and keep enough liquidity to cover a job loss. Which use is best?

options.label: Split it evenly between the card, the car loan, the emergency fund and investments
Put all $10,000 into stock index funds, since expected returns exceed 21% over time
Pay off the card and prepay $7,000 of the car loan to cut total debt
Pay off the card, then put the remaining $7,000 into the emergency fund

rubric: Eliminating the 21% debt and building liquidity toward a three-month buffer satisfies both criteria.
Distractors prepay cheap debt, take unreliable returns or dilute the money without regard to the criteria.

items.prompt: You hold $20,000 in spare cash and a $20,000 loan at 7% fixed. A taxable index fund has an expected 7% pre-tax return, with taxes on gains and year-to-year volatility. Judged on certainty of outcome and after-tax value, which is best?

options.label: Invest in the index fund, since the expected return equals the loan rate and stocks tend to win over long periods
Split the cash evenly, since mixing debt repayment with investing always beats either extreme on risk-adjusted return
Repay the loan, since a guaranteed 7% saving beats an equal expected return that is taxed and uncertain
Keep the cash idle, since liquidity outranks any return from repayment under every circumstance

rubric: Repaying debt gives a certain, effectively tax-free 7% return, which beats an equal expected but taxed and volatile return.
Distractors lean on equal expected returns or always-true rules and ignore risk and tax.

items.prompt: Two households each spend $4,000 a month. Household A has two salaried public-sector earners. Household B has one commission-based earner whose income varies by 40% and who supports a dependent. Judged on income risk, which emergency fund target is best?

options.label: Neither needs a fund, because insurance products cover lost income in all ordinary shortfalls
A needs a larger fund, because two earners spend more freely and face double the chance of job loss
B needs a larger fund, because one volatile income with no second earner leaves bigger shortfalls and longer gaps
Both need the same three months, because equal expenses imply equal fund sizes regardless of income pattern

rubric: Fund size should track income volatility and the lack of a second earner, not expenses alone.
Distractors treat expenses as the only driver or overstate what insurance covers.

items.prompt: A 32-year-old sole earner has two toddlers and a 25-year mortgage, and can spend $120 a month on life insurance. Criteria: the largest death benefit across the dependent years, with a fixed premium. Which option is best?

options.label: A 20-year level term policy with a benefit near ten times income, since it buys the most cover for the years of need
A whole life policy at the largest benefit the budget allows, since coverage lasts forever and builds cash value
A 5-year renewable term policy, since its first-year premium is lowest and renewals are automatic
Employer group cover of one year's salary alone, since it costs nothing and the benefit is easy to keep

rubric: Level term gives the highest cover per dollar for a fixed period matching the dependent years.
Whole life gives far less cover per premium; renewable term premiums rise; group cover is too small and not portable.

items.prompt: A saver's marginal tax rate is 12% now and is expected to be about 24% in retirement 20 years away. Tax on contributions can be paid from other cash. Judged on minimising lifetime tax on this contribution, which is best?

options.label: Taxable account, since avoiding retirement account rules beats any difference in tax rates
Either one, since equal investment growth means the choice never changes lifetime tax
Roth account, since the tax is paid at 12% now instead of at an expected 24% on withdrawal
Traditional account, since a deduction today is always worth more than tax-free growth later

rubric: When the expected future rate exceeds today's, paying tax now (Roth) lowers lifetime tax.
The distractors ignore the rate difference; the 'either one' claim holds only if the two rates are equal.

items.prompt: A 40-year-old wants to retire now with a portfolio of 25 times annual spending, citing the 4% rule, and expects to live 50 more years. Which critique of the plan is strongest?

options.label: The rule is sound at any length, since average market returns are well above 4% over long spans
The rule needs a portfolio of 40 times spending in every case, since it ignores taxes entirely
The rule was tested on roughly 30-year periods, so a 50-year horizon raises failure risk and calls for a lower starting rate
The rule only works for bond-heavy portfolios, so any stock-heavy mix invalidates the 4% figure

rubric: The 4% figure came from about 30-year retirements; a longer horizon exposes the plan to more sequence-of-returns risk.
Distractors invent a fixed 40x requirement, misstate the asset mix, or rely on average returns, which ignore sequence risk.

items.prompt: A planner insists a client in a high-cost city follow the 50/30/20 budget exactly. Which are valid criticisms of that insistence? Select all that apply.

options.label: Needs may exceed 50% of take-home pay where rent is high, so fixed shares can mislead
Irregular costs such as insurance premiums and repairs go unplanned without sinking funds
The rule cannot be used by anyone earning under $100,000 a year
The 20% bucket lumps saving and debt repayment together, hiding that high-rate debt may deserve priority
The percentages must legally be applied to gross income, so the client's numbers are invalid

rubric: Fixed shares ignore local costs, blur debt versus savings priorities, and omit irregular expenses.
The legal-requirement and income-floor claims are invented.

items.prompt: Maya earns $5,000 a month gross. Her employer matches 50% of contributions up to 6% of pay. She owes $8,000 on a card at 22% APR and has $300 in savings. She can free $800 a month. Criteria: maximise guaranteed return and avoid new borrowing. Which plan is best?

options.label: Build a six-month fund first and ignore both the card and match until it is full, since cash comes before everything
Invest all $800 in stocks, since long-run market returns are higher than 22% and the card can wait
Contribute 6% to get the match, put the rest on the card, and keep the $300 as a buffer
Skip the match and send all $800 to the card, since paying 22% interest is always a worse cost than any match

rubric: The match is an immediate 50% return, which beats even 22% debt, and the rest of the surplus should then attack the card.
Distractors reject the match, chase unrealistic stock returns, or delay high-cost debt for a large cash fund.

items.prompt: Design a home for an emergency fund. Constraints: available within one business day, no loss of principal, earns interest, and unaffected by market moves. Which design meets every constraint?

options.label: An insured high-yield savings account at a separate bank, linked for transfers
A five-year CD, since its higher rate outweighs the early-withdrawal penalty on a small balance
Whole life cash value, since policy loans are always available and the balance never falls
A broad stock index fund, since long-run returns beat any savings rate and sales settle in days

rubric: Only an insured savings account meets liquidity, safety, interest and market-independence together.
Stocks risk principal, a CD locks money with a penalty, and cash value loans carry cost and slow growth.

items.prompt: A freelancer's income swings between $2,000 and $9,000 a month. Constraints: $3,500 fixed monthly costs, quarterly estimated tax payments, and no reliance on a good month to pay bills. Which design meets all three?

options.label: Set the salary at the lowest-income-month amount, invest the rest, and leave taxes until the return is filed next spring
Use a credit card limit as the lean-month buffer, repay it in strong months, and pay quarterly tax from any money left
Deposit all income in one account, spend as needed, and settle taxes in one payment at year-end from whatever remains
Pay each receipt into a holding account, set aside a tax share, pay a fixed $3,500 draw, and keep a buffer for lean months

rubric: Separating tax money, a fixed draw and a cash buffer smooths income and funds quarterly payments.
Other designs miss taxes, ignore the $3,500 floor, or rely on borrowing.

items.prompt: A 38-year-old sole earner with a spouse and two children has a 4-month emergency fund, 20-year term life at 10 times income, and a 15% retirement savings rate. Which gap in this plan matters most?

options.label: Extended warranties on major appliances, since they protect the emergency fund from large repair bills
Long-term disability cover replacing part of income, since illness could stop earnings while expenses continue
Paying the mortgage off early from retirement savings, since it removes the largest fixed cost sooner
A whole life policy that adds cash value on top of the term cover, since it also provides permanent protection

rubric: A sole earner's greatest uncovered risk is losing income through disability, which the plan lacks.
The other choices add low-value products or weaken retirement saving.

items.prompt: A couple will buy a home in exactly three years and has $40,000 saved for the down payment. Constraints: principal must be preserved, yield must beat checking, and cash must be available at the purchase date. Which design fits?

options.label: Hold it in a long-dated bond fund, since bonds are safe at any horizon and pay more than savings
A ladder of insured CDs or Treasury bills maturing around the purchase date
Keep it all in checking, since any other choice adds a risk of loss before the purchase
Put all of it in a global stock index fund, since three years is long enough for returns to beat savings

rubric: Maturity-matched, insured fixed-income holdings preserve principal, pay interest, and mature on time.
Stocks and long-duration bond funds can fall in value over three years; checking earns too little.

items.prompt: A homeowner has $6,000 in emergency savings. A higher deductible lowers the premium. Constraints: any single claim must be payable from cash without borrowing, and savings must stay at or above $3,000 afterward. Which deductible gives the lowest total cost within these limits?
rubric: $2,500 is the highest deductible that leaves $3,500, so it saves the most premium within the constraint.
$5,000 would leave only $1,000; lower deductibles cost more in premium.

items.prompt: A single parent of a 7-year-old wants the child protected financially if the parent dies or cannot work. Which elements belong in a plan that meets this goal? Select all that apply.

options.label: Long-term disability insurance replacing part of income
A will naming a guardian and up-to-date beneficiary designations
Credit life insurance on a single car loan
Term life cover lasting until the child is likely independent
A small whole life policy bought as the main investment vehicle

rubric: The goal needs death cover, income protection if disabled, and legal documents to direct assets and guardianship.
A small whole life policy and credit life on one loan do not meet the goal.

items.prompt: Dan and Priya, both 35, earn $110,000 combined and have $1,500 a month of surplus, $12,000 of card debt at 23%, and $1,000 in savings. Priya's employer offers a 100% match on 4% of pay that they have not used. Goals: retire at 62 and fund college in 14 years. Which sequence best meets the goals?

options.label: Invest the whole surplus in stocks, since a 14-year horizon outweighs a 23% interest cost
Fund a college plan first, since its deadline is fixed, and tackle the card debt once the plan is established
Take the match, build a starter fund, clear the card debt, then grow the fund to 3-6 months and save for both goals
Clear all card debt first, skipping the match, then begin saving for retirement and college afterward

rubric: The match gives an immediate 100% return, the debt costs 23%, and a starter fund prevents new borrowing; goals follow.
Distractors skip the match, ignore the debt cost, or put a deadline goal ahead of high-interest debt.
